title: Tally: GCP serverless timesheet and invoicing, terse monologue
proves: Serverless GCP components, month-end calendar, no security or cost discussion.
transcript:
Tally is the timesheet and invoicing tool for our consulting arm. Around four hundred consultants log hours in it every week, and finance runs invoices from it on the first working day of each month.

The front end is a React app served from Firebase Hosting. The API runs on Cloud Run, data is in Cloud SQL for MySQL, and PDF invoices are generated by a Cloud Function and dropped into a Cloud Storage bucket. Cloud Scheduler kicks off the invoice run.

Builds run in Cloud Build on every push to the release branch. Cloud Build deploys a new Cloud Run revision, and if it misbehaves you shift traffic back to the previous revision in the console.

We watch it with Cloud Monitoring and an uptime check on the login page. Errors go to Error Reporting, and the alert policy emails the team when the API's error rate passes two percent for five minutes.

The thing that goes wrong most is the invoice run timing out when a big client has thousands of entries. The fix is to rerun the job for that one client with the client flag set. Also the Cloud SQL connection limit gets hit on Monday mornings when everyone logs their hours at once, and adding a second API instance minimum sorts it out.

Cloud SQL has daily backups kept for thirty days and point-in-time recovery is on. There's no replica in another region, so if europe-west1 goes down we wait for it to come back.

Do not edit the invoices table directly, finance reconciles against it. And never change the Cloud Scheduler timezone, the invoice run moved a day once because of that.

The first working day of the month is the bad one, keep your phone on. Avoid deploying in the last two days of a month.

There is a dev project and a prod project, nothing in between.

The internal tools team owns Tally. Day-to-day questions go to Omar Haddad; for anything with invoices, contact the finance systems lead, Laura Pike.

The move from MySQL 5.7 to 8.0 still needs doing before Google's end of support, and no one has picked it up.

Start by getting the Cloud Run and Cloud SQL viewer roles, then sit in on one invoice run with me.
